chapter: Piano craft and the New York school
title: Tatum, Hines and blind versus visual piano players
summary: Tatum's legato triplets versus visual players like Erroll; how he imitated Hines and judged the keyboard by feel.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Who played piano: the pianists musicians remembered

blocks.x: It almost seemed to me that that was what it was with Earl Hines that... Of course he wasn't blind. But a lot of those things that he did with the left hand where you sort of feared he would never get out of it is...

You see, with Erroll... Like Oscar Peterson told me, he was a visual piano player. See, these people have their eyes, and they play different. Tatum was more a legato. He's in the third, like in the ratio of threes -- he played triplets and all that. Where the other ones I would say are in the ratio of two and four.

But you know how he played, like, the exposition of the melody to begin with, and then he would go into a chorus in the middle where he is... Well, you know on (?) he swings. But that's when you hear Earl's influence in Tatum, in those swing choruses, where...
Well, now, if you're going to hit a piano, where you raise your hand high...

If you have your vision, you can tell exactly where you're going to hit it. Tatum couldn't... He'd raise his hand high simply at the end, because it was a reflex action of some sort. But he couldn't see to really... When he imitated Hines... He used to imitate everybody. When he
imitated Hines, he'd lean over. But he made sure he was in the range of that key before he hit, because he didn't want to miss it. You know what I mean?
Yes. Well, he could imitate everybody...
